body:
Why the pattern of production and consumption matters

Every product requires resources. A mobile phone contains metals, plastics and other materials obtained through extraction and processing. Its manufacture requires energy and water. Transporting, using and eventually disposing of it may create further environmental impacts.

When products are discarded after a short period of use, society must repeatedly extract resources and manufacture replacements. This increases pressure on mineral deposits, forests, water supplies, land and the environment's capacity to absorb pollution.

Natural resources are not all renewed at the same rate. Coal and metallic mineral deposits are effectively non-renewable on human timescales. Water and forests are renewable under suitable conditions, but excessive withdrawal, pollution or destruction can reduce their availability.

Circular economy

A circular economy is an economic approach that seeks to prevent waste and pollution, keep products and materials useful for longer, and support the regeneration of natural systems. It changes how products are designed, produced, used and managed after use.

Linear economy and circular economy

The conventional linear economy is commonly described as taking resources, making products, using them and disposing of them. Its main material flow moves towards waste. A circular economy instead tries to reduce unnecessary resource use and create opportunities for products, components and materials to remain in productive use.

FeatureLinear approachCircular approach
Product designMay give limited attention to repair and recoveryConsiders durability, repair, reuse and recovery
Use of productsFrequently followed by replacementUseful life is extended where practical
Materials after useOften become discarded wasteUseful components and materials are recovered where feasible
Resource demandGreater dependence on repeated virgin extractionAims to reduce demand for virgin resources

The 3 central principles

The circular economy is commonly explained through 3 connected principles:

  • Eliminate waste and pollution: Avoid unnecessary materials, hazardous substances and avoidable waste through better product and system design.
  • Circulate products and materials: Maintain products through reuse, maintenance and repair; recover components and materials when products can no longer serve their original purpose.
  • Regenerate nature: Support natural systems through practices that restore soil health, maintain ecological functions and avoid exhausting renewable resources.

These principles operate together. Recycling an item is useful, but preventing its premature disposal may preserve more of the energy, labour and materials already invested in manufacturing it.

Connection with sustainable development

Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. This understanding was established in the World Commission on Environment and Development report Our Common Future in 1987.

A circular economy is one means of pursuing sustainable development. It mainly improves resource use and production-consumption systems. Sustainable development is broader: it also requires attention to poverty, human welfare, equality and ecological protection.

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 12 concerns responsible consumption and production. Its targets include sustainable and efficient use of natural resources under Target 12.2 and substantial reduction of waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse under Target 12.5, both with a 2030 target year.

Circular does not automatically mean environmentally harmless. Collection, transport, washing, repair and recycling may themselves require resources and produce pollution. The overall environmental outcome depends on the entire system.

Prelims focus

  • A linear economy is associated with resource extraction, production, use and disposal.
  • A circular economy emphasizes waste prevention, circulation of products and materials, and regeneration of natural systems.
  • The Brundtland report, Our Common Future, was published in 1987.
  • SDG 12 concerns responsible consumption and production.
  • SDG Targets 12.2 and 12.5 address resource efficiency and waste reduction respectively.
  • Trap: A circular economy is not simply another name for recycling.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 1, 'Resources', printed pp. 3–6; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, 'Environment and Sustainable Development', sections 9.2 and 9.4; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 9, 'Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context', printed pp. 108–110; United Nations Environment Programme, 'Circularity', section on value-retention processes, consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 'Goal 12', Targets 12.2 and 12.5, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Circular Economy: Meaning, Principles and Sustainable Development

body:
Why circularity begins before a product becomes waste

Many decisions affecting environmental impact are made while a product is being designed. The designer chooses its materials, components, expected service life, method of assembly and means of disassembly. These choices influence how much material is required, whether faults can be repaired and whether the product can be recovered after use.

Design for circularity therefore aims to prevent waste and preserve value from the beginning rather than relying entirely on recycling after disposal.

Durability and repairability

Durability is a product's ability to perform its intended function over time under suitable conditions. A durable product resists premature failure. If it lasts longer, its manufacturing impacts can be spread across more years or units of useful service, provided it remains suitable for use.

Repairability is the ease with which a faulty product can be restored to working condition. A product may be durable but difficult to repair when a component eventually fails.

Repairability improves when designers provide accessible fasteners, replaceable parts, repair information and a construction that can be opened without destroying the product.

Example: An electric fan

A fan with a replaceable switch, accessible wiring and serviceable motor may remain useful after a minor fault. If the same fault requires discarding a sealed, otherwise functional fan, useful materials and components are lost prematurely.

Other important design choices

  • Modular design: Different functional parts can be separated and replaced. A damaged component need not make the whole product unusable.
  • Standardisation: Compatible components, connectors and replacement parts may make maintenance and repair easier.
  • Design for disassembly: Products can be taken apart so that reusable components and recoverable materials are separated without unnecessary damage.
  • Design for reuse: Packaging or equipment is designed to withstand repeated use, cleaning or handling.
  • Design for recycling: Materials are selected and assembled to make their identification, separation and processing practical.
  • Material efficiency: Unnecessary material use and manufacturing losses are reduced while maintaining safety and function.

These choices can reinforce one another, but they may also involve trade-offs. For example, a strong adhesive may improve a product's resistance to moisture while making disassembly more difficult. Design decisions must therefore consider both product performance and recovery after use.

Durability is not the same as biodegradability

A durable material remains functional for a long period. A biodegradable material can be broken down through biological processes under suitable conditions. These are different properties.

Plastic products illustrate the distinction. Many plastics are light, strong and durable, which makes them useful in equipment and packaging. However, discarded plastic can persist in the environment. A material's usefulness during service does not remove the need for responsible waste management.

Similarly, a product described as biodegradable may require particular temperatures, moisture levels or treatment conditions to break down. It should not automatically be treated as harmless when littered in soil or water.

Should an old product always be retained?

Extending product life is generally valuable, but it is not an absolute rule. An exceptionally inefficient old appliance may consume substantially more electricity during use than a suitable replacement. Replacing it might reduce total life-cycle impact, depending on the manufacturing burden of the new appliance, the expected remaining life of the old one and actual usage.

Thus, circular design aims to preserve useful service with lower overall environmental impact, not merely keep every old product in operation indefinitely.

Prelims focus

  • Durability concerns resistance to premature failure.
  • Repairability concerns restoration after failure.
  • Modular design allows individual components to be replaced.
  • Design for disassembly assists component recovery and material separation.
  • Biodegradability and durability describe different material properties.
  • Trap: A long-lasting product is not necessarily easy to repair or recycle.

[Sources: United Nations Environment Programme, 'Circularity', sections 'Reduce by design' and 'Repair', consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations Environment Programme, 'Circularity: Redesigning Systems for a Regenerative Future', section 'Design for Circularity', consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 3, 'Synthetic Fibres and Plastics', sections 3.4–3.6, printed pp. 36–39.]

title: Circular Product Design: Durability, Repairability and Reuse

body:
Different ways of retaining value

A circular economy uses several methods to keep products and materials useful. These methods should not be treated as interchangeable. Some preserve an entire product, some recover its components and others recover only its constituent materials.

In general, keeping a functioning product in use retains more of its existing manufacture, assembly and material value than breaking it down into raw materials. However, the preferable method in an actual case also depends on safety, environmental impact and technical feasibility.

Understanding the main processes

ProcessWhat happensExample
ReuseA product is used again without substantial transformation.A sound glass bottle is returned, cleaned and refilled.
RepairA fault is corrected so that the product works again.A faulty appliance switch is replaced.
RefurbishmentA used product is inspected, cleaned, repaired or upgraded to restore an acceptable condition.A used computer is serviced and prepared for resale.
RemanufacturingA used product is systematically disassembled and rebuilt using inspected, restored or new components to restore as-new or better condition and performance.An industrial motor is rebuilt and tested to an established standard.
RepurposingA product or component is used for a different function.A suitable wooden shipping pallet becomes storage furniture.
RecyclingDiscarded material is processed into material for new production.Recovered aluminium is melted and used to make new products.

Repair, refurbishment and remanufacturing are not identical

Repair focuses on correcting an identified problem. Refurbishment may involve wider cleaning, inspection and replacement of worn parts. Remanufacturing is a more systematic reconstruction process intended to restore as-new or better condition and performance.

For example, replacing a damaged bearing in a motor is a repair. Servicing and restoring several parts of a used motor may constitute refurbishment. Disassembling, inspecting, rebuilding and testing the motor against an established standard may constitute remanufacturing.

These distinctions matter because a used product offered for resale is not automatically remanufactured, and a repaired product has not necessarily been restored to an as-new condition.

Recycling and its limitations

Recycling recovers material rather than preserving the original product. It can reduce demand for virgin resources and divert suitable waste from disposal. Nevertheless, collection, sorting, cleaning and processing require energy and infrastructure.

Materials differ in recyclability. Metals such as aluminium can be recovered and remelted, although collection and processing still create impacts. Many thermoplastics can soften on heating and may be reprocessed under suitable conditions. Thermosetting plastics do not ordinarily soften again after curing, making conventional remelting difficult.

Mixed materials, contamination, additives and poor sorting may reduce recycling quality. Some recycled materials have lower performance or a narrower range of uses than the original material. This is sometimes called downcycling.

Biological cycles and technical cycles

Circular material flows can be considered in 2 broad groups:

  • Biological materials: Suitable organic matter, such as segregated food or agricultural residues, may be composted or processed through controlled biological systems so that useful nutrients return to productive use.
  • Technical materials: Metals, machinery, electronics and many synthetic materials can be maintained, repaired, reused, remanufactured or recycled through suitable industrial processes.

These categories should not be confused with a universal permission to dispose of materials in nature. Composting requires suitable inputs and conditions; contaminated or hazardous materials may require specialised treatment.

Material recovery and energy recovery

Material recovery retains substances for further production. Energy recovery uses suitable waste to obtain heat or electricity, usually through controlled treatment processes. Energy recovery may have a place in residual-waste management, but it does not preserve the original material for continued circulation.

Where environmentally and technically feasible, preventing waste and retaining a functioning product are generally preferable to destroying its material value. Disposal remains necessary for some contaminated or unrecoverable residual waste.

Prelims focus

  • Reuse retains the product without substantial transformation.
  • Repair corrects faults; refurbishment restores general condition.
  • Remanufacturing involves systematic rebuilding to restore as-new or better condition and performance.
  • Recycling converts waste into material for further production.
  • Thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics behave differently on heating.
  • Trap: Energy recovery and material recycling are not the same process.

[Sources: United Nations Environment Programme, 'Circularity', sections on reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing, repurposing and recycling, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 3, 'Synthetic Fibres and Plastics', sections 3.4 and 3.6, printed pp. 36–39; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, 'Environmental Issues', section 16.3, 'Solid Wastes'.]
